The General Insurance Business  
(Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
INTRODUCTION  
§
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972 (the “Act”) was a significant  
legislative development in India's insurance sector as it marked the nationalization of  
general insurance business in the country.  
§
Before the enactment of the Act, the general insurance industry in India was predominantly  
in the hands of private insurance companies. However, the government decided to  
nationalize the sector to provide affordable insurance coverage to a wider section of  
the population, especially in rural areas.  
§
The Act led to the acquisition and transfer of the undertakings of existing general  
insurance companies to the government. It provided for the creation of four  
government-owned insurance companies:  
ü National Insurance Company Ltd.,  
ü New India Assurance Company Ltd.,  
ü Oriental Insurance Company Ltd., and  
ü United India Insurance Company Ltd.  
§
§
§
The Act mandated the transfer of all assets, liabilities, and obligations of the existing  
general insurance companies to the newly formed government-owned companies. Thus,  
this led to the monopoly of the Government in the general insurance sector in India.  
The Act also led to the establishment of the General Insurance Corporation of India  
to control, supervise, and inspect the functioning of the four nationalized insurance  
companies.  
The primary objective of the Act was:  
ü to spread the reach of general insurance services across India, particularly in rural  
and underserved areas;  
ü to provide affordable insurance coverage and promote economic development by  
reducing risks for individuals and businesses;  
ü to ensure that insurance services were available to meet the needs of various  
sectors, including agriculture, industry, trade, and commerce.  
The Act came into force on January 1, 1973.  
§
SOME IMPORTANT DEFINITIONS  
§
Section 3 (a) acquiring company means any Indian insurance company and, where a

§
Section 3 (b) appointed day means such day not being a day later than the 2nd day of

Section 3 (e) existing insurer means every insurer the management of whose undertaking

§
§
Section 3 (f) foreign insurer means an existing insurer incorporated under the law of any

Section 3 (i) Indian insurance company means an existing insurer having a share capital

TRANSFER OF SHARES OF INDIAN INSURANCE COMPANIES SECTION 4  
§
§
§
§
On the appointed day, all the shares in the capital of every Indian insurance company  
shall stand transferred to and vested in the Central Government free of all trusts,  
liabilities and encumbrances affecting them.  
The Central Government will transfer at least ten shares of each of these companies  
to specific individuals through a notification. This transfer will allow these Indian  
insurance companies to operate as Government-owned entities.  
Notification shall specify the names and description of the persons to whom the shares  
are transferred and the particulars of the shares which are transferred to each such  
person.  
A copy of every notification shall be sent by the Central Government to the  
concerned Indian insurance company, who shall rectify its register of members by  
including therein the persons mentioned in the notification as the holders of the shares  
specified therein.  
§
The transfer of shares to the Government won't change any rights the insurance  
company had against shareholders who hadn't paid for their shares, or for any other  
reasons.  
TRANSFER OF UNDERTAKINGS OF OTHER EXISTING INSURERS SECTION 5  
§
On the appointed day, the business of non-Indian insurance companies will be  
transferred to the Central Government which will then decide which Indian insurance  
company will take over that business through a notification.  
§
A notification can state that the business can be transferred to more than one Indian  
insurance company, following certain conditions and guidelines.  
EFFECT OF TRANSFER OF UNDERTAKINGS SECTION 6  
§
The business of every existing insurer mentioned in section 5 shall encompass all their  
assets, rights, powers, properties, cash, funds, investments, and everything connected  
with it. This includes debts, liabilities, and obligations.  
§
All legal documents and agreements involving insurers mentioned in section 5 will  
continue to be valid and enforceable with the Indian insurance company to which  
the business has transferred. They can be executed and enforced as if the Indian  
insurance company was originally a party to these agreements.  
§
If, on the appointed day, there is any ongoing legal case or proceeding related to the  
business of the undertaking which has been transferred under section 5 is pending  
by or against any such existing insurer the same shall not abate, be discontinued  
or be in any way prejudicially affected by reason of the transfer of the undertaking or  
3
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
of anything contained in this Act. Instead, the Indian insurance company to which the  
business has transferred can carry on, pursue, and enforce the case or legal process.  
§
In the case of a foreign insurer or the Life Insurance Corporation, the rules in section 5  
and the preceding sections only apply to property related to their general insurance  
business in India, or in the case of the Life Insurance Corporation, their general insurance  
business worldwide. This includes rights, powers, debts, liabilities, contracts, agreements,  
and legal proceedings related to this specific business.  
TRANSFER OF SERVICE OF EXISTING EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN CASES SECTION 7  
§
Every full-time officer or employee of an existing insurer, excluding Indian insurance  
companies, who was primarily engaged in the general insurance business before the  
appointed day, will automatically become an officer or employee of the Indian  
insurance company in which that insurer's business has been transferred. They will  
retain their position under the Indian insurance company with the same terms, including  
rights to pension and gratuity, as if there had been no transfer. This arrangement  
continues unless their employment is terminated by the Indian insurance company, or until  
his remuneration, terms and conditions are duly altered by that Indian insurance company.  
However, if an officer or employee provides written notice to the Central Government or  
its nominee before the appointed day, expressing their intention not to join the Indian  
insurance company, this rule does not apply to them.  
§
§
If any question arises as to whether any person was a whole-time officer or employee, or  
as to whether any officer or employee, was employed wholly or mainly in connection with  
the general insurance business of the existing insurer before a certain date, it shall be  
sent to the Central Government within two years from that date.  
§
When the services of an officer or employee are transferred, they shall not be eligible for  
compensation under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, or any other law. Courts,  
Tribunals, or authorities shall not entertain such claims.  
PROVIDENT, SUPERANNUATION, WELFARE AND OTHER FUNDS SECTION 8  
§
§
§
Where an existing insurer has established a provident, superannuation, welfare, or any  
other fund for the benefit of his employees and constituted a trust for that (existing trust),  
all the money in that fund on the appointed day, together with any other assets belonging  
to such fund, shall stand transferred to and vested in the Indian insurance company  
on the appointed day free from any such trust.  
Where all the employees of the Life Insurance Corporation or any other existing insurer  
do not become employees of an Indian insurance company, the money and other assets  
belonging to any such fund, shall be apportioned between the trustees of the fund and  
the Indian insurance company; and in case of any dispute about such apportionment  
the decision of the Central Government thereon shall be final.  
Where the undertaking of an existing insurer has vested in more than one Indian  
insurance company, the Central Government may provide for the apportionment  
4
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
among such Indian insurance companies of money and other assets belonging to any  
existing trust relating to that undertaking.  
§
§
The Indian insurance company shall, as soon as may be after the appointed day  
constitute in respect of the moneys and other assets which are transferred to and vested  
in it one or more trusts having objects as similar to the objects of the existing trusts.  
Where all the money and other assets belonging to an existing trust are transferred to and  
vested in an Indian insurance company, the trustees of such trust shall, as from the  
appointed day, stand discharged from the trust, except as respects things done or  
omitted to be done before the appointed day.  
FORMATION OF GENERAL INSURANCE CORPORATION OF INDIA SECTION 9  
§
§
The Central Government shall form the General Insurance Corporation of India for the  
purpose of superintending, controlling, and carrying on the business of general  
insurance.  
The authorised capital of the Corporation shall be rupees two hundred and fifty  
crores, divided into two hundred and fifty lakhs fully paid-up shares of one hundred  
rupees each, out of which rupees five crores shall be the initial subscribed capital of  
the Corporation.  
§
It shall not be necessary to add the word Limited as the last word of the name of the  
Corporation.  
TRANSFER TO CORPORATION OF SHARES VESTED IN CENTRAL GOVERNMENT  
SECTION 10  
§
All shares of Indian insurance companies transferred to the Central Government as per  
Section 4, except those given to specific individuals, will be transferred to and vested  
in the Corporation. The insurance companies must update their records to show the  
Corporation as the shareholder of these shares.  
TRANSFER TO CENTRAL GOVERNMENT OF SHARES VESTED IN CORPORATION  
SECTION 10A  
§
All the shares in the capital of the acquiring companies, being:  
ü the National Insurance Company Limited;  
ü the New India Assurance Company Limited;  
ü the Oriental Insurance Company Limited;  
ü the United India Insurance Company Limited,  
and vested in the Corporation before the commencement of the General Insurance  
Business (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 2002 shall, on such commencement, stand  
transferred to the Central Government.

The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
ENHANCEMENT OF EQUITY CAPITAL OF GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANIES SECTION  
10B  
§
The General Insurance Corporation and the insurance companies specified in section 10A  
may, raise their capital for:  
ü increasing their business in rural and social sectors,  
ü to meet solvency margin and  
ü such other purposes, as the Central Government may empower in this behalf.  
AMOUNTS TO BE PAID FOR TRANSFER AND VESTING OF SHARES OR UNDERTAKINGS  
SECTION 11  
§
For the transfer of the shares of each Indian insurance company to, and vesting in, the  
Central Government, the Central Government shall pay to the Corporation, for  
distribution to the shareholders of each such company, the amount specified against  
such company in the corresponding entry under column (3) of Part A of the Schedule.  
For the transfer to, and vesting in the Central Government, of the undertaking of each  
existing insurer, who is not an Indian insurance company, the Central Government shall  
pay to the Corporation, for payment to each such existing insurer, the amount specified  
against such insurer in the corresponding entry under column (3) of Part B of the  
Schedule.  
§
DISBURSEMENT OF AMOUNTS BY CORPORATION SECTION 12  
§
§
The total amount paid by the Central Government under section 11 shall be treated as  
additional contribution to the subscribed capital of the Corporation and it shall stand  
allotted to, and vested in, the Central Government.  
The Corporation shall distribute the amount received under Section 11 to the  
shareholders of Indian insurance companies and existing insurers, based on their  
rights and interests. In case of any doubt or dispute about who should receive the money,  
the Corporation will refer the matter to the Central Government for a decision and then  
follow the Government's decision.  
MODE OF PAYMENT SECTION 13  
§
Where the amount referred to in section 11 is to be given:  
ü to the members of an Indian insurance company, the amount due to each such  
member shall be paid in full, where it does not exceed twenty-five thousand  
rupees, and where it exceeds twenty-five thousand rupees, each such member  
shall be paid twenty-five thousand rupees and the balance of the amount due to  
such member shall be paid to him in three equal annual instalments, the first  
of which shall fall due on the appointed day;  
ü to a foreign insurer, it shall be given to him in cash within three months from  
the appointed day;  
ü to the Life Insurance Corporation, it shall be given to it in three equal annual  
instalments, the first of which shall fall due on the appointed day;  
6
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
ü to an existing insurer who is a co-operative society, it shall be distributed as  
soon as may be after the appointed day in accordance with the rules of the  
society which will apply in case of dissolution of the society;  
ü to an existing insurer not falling within any of the foregoing provisions, it shall  
be apportioned by the acquiring company among the individual policy-holders of  
the insurer whose policies with that insurer were in force on the appointed day and  
were comprised in the undertaking of such insurer in proportion to the premiums  
paid by the policy-holders under such policies and every such payment shall be  
made either:  
•
•
in cash, to be sent by postal money order, or  
at the option of the policy-holder, as a deduction in the premium due at the  
time of the renewal of the policy and such option shall be exercised by the  
policy-holder before the expiry of three months from the appointed day (or  
within such further time not exceeding three months as the Central  
Government may, on the application of the policy-holder, allow); and the  
option so exercised shall be final and shall not be altered or rescinded after  
it has been exercised:  
If any policy-holder fails to exercise his option within the time allowed, he shall be  
deemed to have exercised his option in favour of payment in cash by postal  
money order.  
§
Where any amount is payable whether in instalments or otherwise, the unpaid  
amount, where its payment has become due shall carry interest at the rate of four per  
cent per annum from the appointed day.  
AMOUNT PAYABLE TO SHAREHOLDERS MAY BE PAID TO NAMED PERSONS INSTEAD  
IN CERTAIN CASES SECTION 14  
§
If a majority of the members of an Indian insurance company, representing at least two-  
thirds of the company's value, agree at a specially convened meeting before the  
appointed day, that the amount payable to the company's members can be given to a  
person or group nominated by those members for conducting a business.  
The Central Government may approve this if it's satisfied that those who disagree with  
this decision will still be compensated for their shares and may also determine the  
conditions for this transfer.  
§
§
No resolution passed at any such meeting as mentioned above and held after the  
appointed day shall have any effect unless the meeting has been convened after  
obtained the approval of the Central Government.  
PAYMENT INTO COURT IN CASE OF RIVAL CLAIMS SECTION 15  
§
Where a claim to the amount payable under section 11 is made by two or more persons  
adversely to one another, the corporation may cause the amount to be deposited in  
7
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
any civil court having jurisdiction in that behalf and the Court shall decide as to whom  
the payment shall be made.  
SCHEMES FOR MERGERS OF COMPANIES, ETC. SECTION 16  
§
If the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary for the efficient operation  
of general insurance, it can create one or more schemes through notifications  
providing various aspects, such as:  
ü Merging Indian insurance companies or forming new ones through  
amalgamation: the merger in one Indian insurance company of any other Indian  
insurance company, or the formation of a new company by the amalgamation of  
two or more Indian insurance companies;  
ü Transferring assets, liabilities, and business from one company to another:  
the transfer to and vesting in the acquiring company of the undertaking (including  
all its business, properties, assets and liabilities) of any Indian insurance company  
which ceases to exist by reason of the scheme;  
ü Defining the acquiring company's structure, capital, and management  
Board: the constitution, name and registered office and the capital structure of the  
acquiring company and the issue and allotment of shares;  
ü Modifying the acquiring company's Articles and Memorandum: the alteration  
of the memorandum and articles of association of the acquiring company for such  
purposes as may be necessary to give effect to the scheme;  
ü Retaining the services and terms of employment for employees: the  
continuance in the acquiring company of the services of all officers and other  
employees of the Indian insurance company which has ceased to exist by reason  
of the scheme, on the same terms and conditions which they were getting or, as  
the case may be, by which they were governed immediately before the  
commencement of the scheme;  
ü Adjusting pay scales and terms of service as needed: the rationalisation or  
revision of pay scales and other terms and conditions of service of officers and  
other employees wherever necessary;  
ü Transferring employee funds like provident and superannuation: the transfer  
to the acquiring company of the provident, superannuation, welfare and other  
funds relating to the officers and other employees of the Indian insurance company  
which has ceased to exist by reason of the scheme;  
ü Managing legal proceedings involving the company: the continuance by or  
against the acquiring company of legal proceedings pending by or against any  
Indian insurance company which has ceased to exist by reason of the scheme,  
and the initiation of such legal proceedings, civil or criminal, as the Indian  
insurance company might have initiated if it had not ceased to exist;  
ü Handling any necessary additional matters to make the scheme effective:  
such incidental, consequential and supplemental matters as are necessary to give  
full effect to the scheme.  
8
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
§
§
§
In framing schemes, the object of the Central Government shall be to ensure that  
ultimately there are up to four companies (excluding the Corporation) in existing and that  
they are so situate as to render their combined services effective in all parts of India.  
Where a scheme provides for the transfer of any property or liabilities, then, by virtue of  
the scheme, the property shall stand transferred to and vested in, and those liabilities  
shall be transferred to and become the liabilities of, the acquiring company.  
If the rationalisation or revision of any pay scale or other terms and conditions of service  
under any scheme is not acceptable to any officer or other employee, the acquiring  
company may terminate his employment by giving him compensation equivalent to  
three months' remuneration, unless the contract of service with such employee  
provides for a shorter notice of termination.  
§
Regardless of the Industrial Disputes Act of 1947 or any other laws in place, when an  
officer or employee from an Indian insurance company is transferred to the acquiring  
company, they will not be entitled to compensation under these laws, and any claims  
in this regard will not be entertained by Courts, Tribunals, or Authorities.  
§
§
The Central Government may, by notification, add to, amend, or vary any scheme framed.  
The power to frame a scheme, and the power to add to, amend or vary any scheme framed  
under this section, shall include the power to frame such scheme with retrospective  
effect from a date not earlier than the appointed day.  
FUNCTIONS OF CORPORATION SECTION 18  
§
The functions of the Corporation shall include:  
ü the carrying on of any part of the general insurance business, if it thinks it desirable  
to do so;  
ü aiding, assisting and advising the acquiring companies in the matter of setting up  
of standards of conduct and sound practice in general insurance business and in  
the matter of rendering efficient service to holders of policies of general insurance;  
ü advising the acquiring companies in the matter of controlling their expenses  
including the payment of commission and other expenses;  
ü advising the acquiring companies in the matter of the investment of their funds;  
ü issuing directions to acquiring companies in relation to the conduct of general  
insurance business:  
•
all the functions of the Corporation specified in this sub-section, on and  
from the commencement of the General Insurance Business  
(Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 2002, shall be performed by the Central  
Government.  
ü In issuing any directions the Central Government shall keep in mind the desirability  
of encouraging competition amongst the acquiring companies as far as  
possible in order to render their services more efficient.  
FUNCTIONS OF ACQUIRING COMPANIES SECTION 19  
9
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
§
Subject to any rules established by the Central Government and following its  
memorandum and articles of association, each acquiring company is obligated to  
engage in the business of general insurance.  
§
§
Every acquiring company must conduct general insurance business, following the  
Central Government's rules and its own memorandum and articles of association.  
When performing its functions, each acquiring company should generally follow  
business principles. If the Central Government or the Insurance Regulatory and  
Development Authority has issued any specific directions, the company should also  
follow those directions.  
BALANCE OF PROFIT HOW TO BE UTILISED SECTION 20  
§
After setting aside money for various expenses like bad debts, asset depreciation,  
employee funds, government debts, and other necessary provisions, the acquiring  
company will distribute the remaining profits as dividends.  
INTERIM PROVISIONS FOR MANAGEMENT OF INDIAN INSURANCE COMPANIES  
SECTION 21  
§
From the appointed day and until a new Board of directors is established for an Indian  
insurance company, the Custodian in charge of managing the company's affairs  
under the General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1971, will retain control. The  
Custodian will have the authority, with guidance from the Central Government, to exercise  
all the powers and perform the actions typically done by the company or its Board of  
directors.  
§
§
The above provision shall not prevent the Central Government from appointing  
someone else to manage the affairs of an Indian insurance company if needed  
during the mentioned period. The appointed person can exercise the same powers and  
perform the same actions as a Custodian.  
The Custodian and the person appointed shall be entitled to salaries and other  
allowances as the Central Government may specify and shall hold office during the  
pleasure of the Central Government.  
ACQUIRING COMPANIES TO HAVE THE EXCLUSIVE PRIVILEGE OF CARRYING ON  
GENERAL INSURANCE BUSINESS SECTION 24  
§
§
On and from the appointed day, the Corporation and the acquiring companies shall have  
the exclusive privilege of carrying on general insurance business in India.  
Except for insurers mentioned above and subject to section 36, any registration  
certificate issued under the Insurance Act will become invalid starting from the  
appointed day.  
10  
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
ü nothing as mentioned in the above provision shall apply to the carrying on by the  
Life Insurance Corporation of life insurance business and capital redemption and  
annuity certain business.  
EXCLUSIVE PRIVILEGE OF CORPORATION AND ACQUIRING COMPANIES TO CEASE  
SECTION 24A  
§
The exclusive privilege of the Corporation and the acquiring companies to conduct general  
insurance business in India will end when the Insurance Regulatory and Development  
Authority Act, 1999 comes into effect. After that, the Corporation and acquiring  
companies will continue their general insurance business in India following the rules of the  
Insurance Act, 1938.  
ü the Corporation shall, on and from the commencement of the General Insurance  
Business (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 2002, cease to carry on general  
insurance business.  
ACQUIRING COMPANIES AND INCOME-TAX SECTION 26  
§
Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, every acquiring company will be considered as both:  
ü an Indian company and  
ü a company in which the public are significantly interested.  
RIGHT OF ACQUIRING COMPANY TO SEEK RELIEF IN RESPECT OF CERTAIN  
TRANSACTIONS SECTION 28  
§
Where an existing insurer has at any time within five years before the 13th day of  
May, 1971:  
ü made any payment to any person without consideration,  
ü sold or disposed of any property of the insurer without consideration or for an  
inadequate consideration,  
ü acquired any property or rights for an excessive consideration,  
ü entered into or varied any agreement so as to require an excessive consideration  
to be paid or given by the insurer,  
ü entered into any other transaction of such an onerous nature as to cause a loss to,  
or impose a liability on, the insurer exceeding any benefit accruing to the insurer,  
and the payment, sale, disposal, acquisition, agreement, or any other transaction made  
by an insurer was not reasonably necessary for its general insurance business or  
lacked prudence, the acquiring company can seek relief from the Court regarding that  
transaction. All parties involved in the transaction should be included in the application  
unless the court decides otherwise.  
DUTY TO DELIVER POSSESSION OF PROPERTY AND DOCUMENTS RELATING THERETO  
SECTION 29  
§
Where any property appertaining to an existing insurer has been transferred to and vested  
in an Indian insurance company under section 5:  
11  
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
ü every person in whose possession, custody or control any such property may be,  
shall deliver the property to the Indian insurance company forthwith,  
ü any person who immediately before such vesting has in his possession, custody  
or control any books, documents or other papers relating to an existing insurer  
shall be liable to account for the said books, documents, and papers to the Indian  
insurance company, and shall deliver them to that company or to such person as  
that company may direct.  
§
All the assets of an existing insurer appertaining to the undertaking held in deposit by the  
Reserve Bank of India under the Insurance Act or by trustees in trust shall be delivered  
to the Indian insurance company.  
PENALTY FOR WITHHOLDING PROPERTY, ETC. SECTION 30  
§
If any person wilfully withholds or fails to deliver property, books, documents, or papers to  
an Indian insurance company as required by section 29, or wrongfully keeps property  
transferred to the Indian insurance company for purposes not allowed by this Act, they  
can be punished, upon complaint by the Indian insurance company, with imprisonment  
for up to one year, a fine of up to one thousand rupees, or both.  
DISSOLUTION OF CORPORATION AND ACQUIRING COMPANIES SECTION 33  
§
The Corporation and acquiring companies are exempt from company winding-up laws.  
They can only be placed in liquidation if the Central Government orders it and  
specifies the process.  
EXEMPTION SECTION 36  
Nothing contained in this Act shall apply in relation to:  
§
ü any general insurance business conducted by a State Government, especially  
concerning its properties or entities owned or significantly funded by the State  
Government, is excluded from certain provisions;  
ü any general insurance business not falling under the above category which has  
been carried on by a State Government before the commencement of this Act, to  
the extent to which it is necessary to allow such business to run off:  
•
nothing contained in this clause shall be deemed to authorise the State  
Government to issue any new policies or renew any existing policies;  
ü any insurer whose business is being voluntarily wound up or is being wound up by  
a court;  
ü the insurance business carried on by the Calcutta Hospital and Nursing Home  
Benefits Association Limited;  
12  
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972  
ü the insurance business carried on by the Export Credit and Guarantee Corporation  
Limited and the Deposit Insurance Corporation established under section 3 of the  
Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, 1961;  
ü any scheme in existence immediately before the 14th day of May, 1971 or any  
scheme framed after the said day with the approval of the Central Government for  
the insurance of crops or of cattle or of flood risks or of war or emergency risks.  
§
If the Central Government is satisfied that an insurer, whether established before or  
after the appointed day, carries on only such general insurance business as is not  
carried on ordinarily by insurers, it may, by notification, direct that nothing contained in  
this Act shall apply to such insurer.
